summary: LunaricB answers a question mission planners face whenever a schedule moves: if launch slips by a week, what does the lander lose on the Moon? For any south-polar landing site and date, it computes from real LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides when the Sun is above the local horizon (power) and when Earth is visible (direct communication), hour by hour across the surface mission. Two plans can be compared side by side, for example the same site one week apart, or two sites on the same date. At Mons Mouton, a landing on 30 Nov 2028 keeps the Sun in view 99.8% of the window; one week later that drops to 30.4%. The tool shows the trade before the decision is made.
details:
LunaricB is a browser-based landing site navigator for the lunar south pole. It answers a question mission planners face whenever a schedule moves: if launch slips by a week, what does the lander lose on the Moon?

How it works: For a chosen site, we build the local horizon from NASA LOLA digital elevation models (PGDA 80 m and 240 m polar mosaics, plus 5 m site tiles), tracing 720 azimuths out to 300 km. Sun and Earth positions come from the JPL Horizons API in the Moon's mean-Earth frame. For every hour of the mission we compute the visible fraction of the Sun's disc (power) and whether Earth's centre is above the terrain (direct-to-Earth link). Results appear as a mission timeline, a horizon panorama, and a 3D view of the real terrain lit by the true Sun direction, with earthshine, a phase-correct Earth and the real star field.

Comparison: Two plans (dates or sites) are shown side by side with a one-line verdict, so a team sees what a slip or a site change costs in sunlit hours and Earth-contact hours. Example: at Mons Mouton, a landing on 30 Nov 2028 keeps the Sun in view 99.8% of the window; one week later it drops to 30.4%.

Validation: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to 0.0002° and 0.006°. Illumination results agree with Barker et al. (2021, Planetary and Space Science 203): 86.85% vs 86.81% for a published case, and 87.34% vs 86.61% averaged at 5 m resolution. Moving a site by only 160 m raised 2027 illumination from 82.9% to 90.1%.

Tools: JavaScript, three.js, Python for terrain preprocessing; hosted on GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/demonszy07/lunarplanb

Limits: Terrain resolution limits accuracy for very small features; the tool reports line-of-sight visibility, not link budgets or thermal models.

Use of AI: I used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant to write most of the code, under my direction. I defined the problem and the approach, chose the data sources, designed the validation against JPL Horizons and Barker et al. (2021), reviewed and tested the results, and made the design and product decisions. No AI-generated images are presented as NASA data.
